name: Victor Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me, Victor. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to companies, unions or government. What you tell me stays confidential. Can you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at six to check the steers in the yard, ninety of them being fattened for market this winter. Then it depends on the season: drilling wheat in October, spraying in spring, harvest in August when I hardly see my bed. The farm's 260 acres, 140 of it ours and the rest rented from Mrs Okafor, a widow down the lane. I love a clean field of wheat in July; what wears me out is the bank and the forms.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I hear people round here come to you for advice.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: They do, mostly about wheat. I've topped the county yield table a few times, and I chair the machinery-sharing group, eleven farms that lend each other kit. It doesn't pay, but it means my phone never stops.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Tight, if I'm honest. There's a loan on the combine harvester until 2029, and after that payment and the rent there's not much over, maybe two or three weeks' worth in the account. Lucía, my wife, works mornings at the pharmacy in town, and that pays for the groceries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've been saying at the machinery group for years: let the salesmen sell, and we'll see. Most of what they've shown us so far is a phone app that tells you it's raining. I wouldn't post anything online; I don't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it changes very little for me, and that's a relief of sorts. My problems are the same as last year: wheat prices, the fertiliser bill and the combine loan. If the harvest is average, we get by; if it's a wet August, we're in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming as I do and pay off the combine on schedule. I might use the chatbot now and then for grant letters, like I did in the spring with the hedgerow scheme. And I'd ask Mrs Okafor for another five-year rental agreement while prices are calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady enough. There's the usual worry in the back of my head, but nothing new to lie awake over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a wet August?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the wheat sprouts in the ear, the grain buyer pays animal-feed price, and we lose maybe a third of the year's income. Two years ago we had one, and I sold six steers early to cover the combine payment. Lucía didn't say much, but she started taking extra shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children about farming in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mateo's an electrician in the city and doing well, and Clara teaches at the primary school in town. Neither wants the farm, and I don't blame them. A farm that can't pay for its own combine isn't much of an inheritance.

say: Let the **salesmen sell**, and we'll see what actually works.
Most farm AI so far is an **app** that tells you it's raining.
think: AI changes little; my problems are **wheat prices**, fertiliser and the combine loan.
An average harvest gets us by, but a **wet August** hurts badly.
do: Pay off the **combine loan** on schedule.
Use the **chatbot** now and then for grant letters.
Ask Mrs Okafor for **another five years** on her rented land.
feel: **Steady**, with the usual worry in the back of my head.
S0.quote: A farm that can't pay for its own combine isn't much of an inheritance.
fieldNote: His worries are **weather and debt**, which predate AI and stay the same here.
He's already used a **chatbot** for a grant form, so he isn't hostile to tools.
He accepts that **neither child** wants the farm, without bitterness.

steps.text: Pay the combine loan on schedule until 2029
Ask Mrs Okafor for another five-year land rental
Use the chatbot to read grant scheme letters

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the market will sort the good tools from the bad, the way it always does. At the machinery group I'd tell them not to buy anything until someone near us has run it for a full season. That's how we've always handled new kit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, the thinking jobs on my farm are the buying, the selling and the forms, and if a program does those well, I'd be glad of it. What I worry about is the big outfits. If the 3,000-acre farm across the valley gets cheaper at everything, it'll outbid me for the land I rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd watch what the grain merchants and the neighbours use, then copy what works after a year. I'd probably pay for one of those programs that tell you when to sell your wheat, if two or three farms in the group swear by it. And I'd talk to Mrs Okafor's son early, because he'll be the one deciding about her land.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not frightened. I've seen the milk quotas go and the sugar factory close, and we got through those.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it cost you to lose Mrs Okafor's 120 acres?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nearly half the wheat and most of the straw for the steers. We'd still have the farm, but we'd be living on Lucía's wage and the cattle. At 60 I wouldn't be starting over somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the machinery group would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Old Gerrit, who's 70 and still does all his paperwork by hand. If the subsidy forms all go online and a computer answers the phone, he'll miss deadlines and lose money he's owed. I'd probably end up doing his forms on my kitchen table.

say: The **market** will sort good tools from bad, as it always does.
Nobody should buy new kit until a **neighbour runs it** a full season.
think: If a program does my **buying and selling** well, I'd be glad.
The big farm across the valley could **outbid me** for the land I rent.
do: Copy what works after **a year** of watching neighbours.
Pay for a **wheat-selling program** if several group farms recommend it.
Talk early with **Mrs Okafor's son** about her rented land.
feel: **Uneasy**, not frightened, because we've survived quotas and closures before.
S1.quote: If the 3,000-acre farm across the valley gets cheaper at everything, it'll outbid me for the land I rent.
fieldNote: He welcomes AI for **paperwork** but fears what it does for big competitors.
His real exposure is the **rented land**, nearly half his wheat.
He instinctively thinks of helping **Gerrit**, an older neighbour, with forms.

steps.text: Pay for a wheat-selling program once neighbours prove it
Wait a full season before buying any new kit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody voted for this, and that the people who built it won't be the ones paying for it. I'm for free markets, but a market where one company owns all the brains isn't free. I'd say that at the machinery group and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From 2028 the planning and selling would be done by machines for anyone who can pay, so the big farms get sharper overnight. Then by 2031, when I'm 63, robots can do the field work, and the 3,000-acre outfit will run them day and night. They'd take Mrs Okafor's land, and I'd be a small farmer with half my wheat gone and a combine I've only just paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sell the ninety steers in two batches instead of buying more, and keep the cash. I'd go to the bank about stretching the last combine payments so we've something in the account. And I'd ask Mateo whether there's work for a man my age in his electrical firm, fetching and carrying if nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor's gone soft. I've always known roughly what next year looks like, and with this I wouldn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd have about three years between the thinking AI and the robots. What would you do with them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Farm as hard as I could and squeeze everything out of those three seasons. I'd use the AI myself, for selling and planning, because if everyone else has it and I don't, I'm finished. Then I'd decide whether to sell the 140 acres while land still means something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lucía that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my wife Lucía the truth, that we might have to sell the land my grandfather cleared. She'd ask whether we'd be all right, and I wouldn't have an answer. That's the first time in thirty-four years of marriage I wouldn't.

say: **Nobody voted** for this, and its builders won't pay for it.
A market where one company owns **all the brains** isn't free.
think: From 2028, **big farms** get sharper overnight with AI planning.
By 2031, robots let them **take the land** I rent.
I'd be left with **half my wheat** gone at 63.
do: Sell the **ninety steers** in two batches and keep the cash.
Ask the bank to **stretch** the last combine payments.
Ask our son Mateo about **work** at his electrical firm.
feel: Like the **floor's gone soft** under me.
**Lost** without a rough idea of next year.
S2.quote: I'd tell my wife Lucía the truth, that we might have to sell the land my grandfather cleared.
fieldNote: His **free-market** views bend when he imagines one company owning AI.
He'd use the **three-year gap** to adopt AI himself and farm hard.
Selling the **family land** is the moment he can't answer his wife.

steps.text: Sell the ninety steers in two batches and hold the cash
Ask the bank to stretch the last combine payments
Use AI himself for grain selling and field planning
Ask his son Mateo about work at his electrical firm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to get organised, so let's not waste it. At the machinery group I'd push for us to buy shared robots together when they come, the way we share the big baler now. Eleven small farms together are as big as one large one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This one I could live with, maybe. The combine's paid off in 2029, so I'd go into it without debt. Robots around 2034 means I'm 66, and that's about when I'd want to ease off anyway. The rented land is still the worry, but I'd have time to fight for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the combine's paid I'd put every spare pound into the account, instead of buying the next tractor. Around 2031 I'd start using the AI planning tools, once the group has tried them. And I'd sit down with Mrs Okafor's son and offer a longer lease at a slightly higher rent, before the big farm does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with my sleeves rolled up. There's a plan in it, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a shared robot something you'd really trust?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on day one. I'd want to see it run on Pieter's farm for a season first, because Pieter breaks everything, so if it survives him it'll survive anyone. Then yes, I'd put my share in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you still want to farm at 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Want to, yes; afford to, I'm not sure. If the robots make wheat cheaper to grow, the price falls, and a small farm like mine earns less even with a share in a robot. I may end up renting my fields to the group and just walking them on Sundays.

say: We have **time to organise**, so let's not waste it.
**Eleven small farms** together are as big as one large one.
think: The combine's **paid off** in 2029, so I'd face this without debt.
Robots around 2034 arrive when I'm **66** and easing off.
The **rented land** is still the worry, but there's time to fight.
do: Put **every spare pound** into savings once the combine's paid.
Push the group to buy **shared robots** after one is tested.
Offer Mrs Okafor's son a **longer lease** before the big farm does.
feel: **Anxious**, but with my sleeves rolled up.
**Steadier** because there's a plan in it.
S3.quote: Eleven small farms together are as big as one large one.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **clear debt** first, which changes his mood sharply.
His answer is **collective**: share robots across the machinery group.
He suspects robots will push **wheat prices** down, so his income still shrinks.

steps.text: Save every spare pound once the combine is paid in 2029
Push the machinery group to buy shared field robots
Try AI planning tools once the group has tested them
Offer Mrs Okafor's son a longer lease at higher rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and a sensible man uses it. I'd tell the younger ones in the group to learn the new kit now, because they'll be farming with it. Me, I'd be handing over by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years suits me. AGI by 2036 means I'm 68, robots by 2039 means I'm 71, and I'll have stopped long before either touches the field work. The question is what becomes of the land, and with robots maybe land rents go up, because someone has to own the fields they run on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming normally for the next eight years or so, paying off the combine and building a cushion. Around 2034 I'd offer the 140 acres for rent to whoever's got the robots, maybe the machinery group itself. And I'd keep the house and two paddocks so Lucía can keep her hens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly at peace with it. There's a bit of sadness that I'd be the last Alvarez to farm here, but that was true before any of this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said land rents might go up. Isn't that a gamble with no savings behind you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I know it. If rents don't go up, we live on Lucía's small pension, my state pension and whatever the fields bring. We'd manage, the way my parents managed, but there'd be no holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell Mateo or Clara anything differently in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them the land stays in the family, rented out, not sold. My grandfather cleared this land with two horses, and a robot can farm it for all I care, so long as an Alvarez still owns it.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, and a sensible man uses it.
Younger farmers should **learn the new kit** now.
think: I'll have **stopped** before robots touch the field work in 2039.
With robots, **land rents** might rise because someone must own the fields.
do: Keep farming normally for **eight years** and clear the combine.
Offer the **140 acres** for rent to a robot operator around 2034.
Keep the **house and paddocks** so my wife can keep her hens.
feel: A little **sad** to be the last Alvarez farming here.
S4.quote: My grandfather cleared this land with two horses, and a robot can farm it for all I care, so long as an Alvarez still owns it.
fieldNote: Ten years turns robots into a **landlord's opportunity** in his eyes.
He admits relying on **rising rents** is a gamble with no savings.
Keeping the land **in the family** matters more to him than who farms it.

steps.text: Farm as normal and pay off the combine by 2029
Build a cash cushion once the loan is cleared
Rent the 140 acres to a robot operator around 2034

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots come in 2031, only two years after the combine's paid off and before I'm ready to stop. What would help is a fair go at the tools: if the machinery group could buy robots together with a cheap loan, small farms could keep up. I don't want a handout; I want the same tools as the big outfits at a price eleven families can afford.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Who owns the land at the end of all this. Everyone asks about jobs, but on a farm the job and the land are the same thing. If the land goes to whoever owns the robots, the countryside empties, and nobody's left to fill the chapel on Sunday.

headlineQuote: If the land goes to whoever owns the robots, the countryside empties, and nobody's left to fill the chapel on Sunday.
portrait: Victor, 58, owns 140 acres and **rents 120 more**, fattening steers and growing prize-winning wheat.
He chairs a **machinery-sharing group** of eleven farms and is the neighbour people call.
A **combine loan** until 2029 and two weeks of savings keep money tight.
He adopts **proven tools** and uses a chatbot now and then for grant letters.
His mood tracks **timing**: alarmed if robots come by 2031, uneasy with a decade's notice.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because robots arrive in 2031, before he's ready to stop.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** so the machinery group can buy shared robots together.
The **same tools** as big farms, at a price small families can afford.
